title: The drinking bird isn't perpetual motion: it's a heat engine run by evaporation

cover.alt: A toy drinking bird with a blue top hat and green tail feathers tipped forward, its red beak dipped into a glass of water.

body: A drinking bird is two glass bulbs joined by a tube, emptied of air and holding a volatile liquid, usually dichloromethane, plus its vapour. Water evaporating from the felt on its head cools the head, so some vapour inside condenses and the pressure there drops. The warmer vapour in the body then pushes liquid up the neck until the bird turns top-heavy and tips forward to 'drink'. That lets a bubble of warm vapour up the tube, the pressures even out and the liquid drains back. Like any heat engine, it runs on a temperature difference: between its wet head and the slightly warmer air around it.

slides.alt: A toy drinking bird next to a glass of water slowly leans further and further forward until its beak dips into the water, then swings back upright and rocks to and fro.
slides.caption: The bird leans slowly forward until its beak dips into the water, then swings back upright and rocks, ready to start the cycle again.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: It runs on a temperature difference
Its glass body is full of air
The liquid inside is often dichloromethane

slides.explanation: The air is pumped out, leaving only the liquid and its vapour. The bird keeps going only while evaporation keeps its head cooler than the room.

slides.question: Where does the energy that keeps the bird bobbing come from?
options: A battery hidden in the base
slides.explanation: Evaporation keeps the head cooler, while the warmer room heats the liquid in the body. Heat flowing from warm to cool drives the cycle, as in any heat engine.
